lede: Plants take mineral ions out of the soil even when there is more inside the root than outside, and that uphill journey costs energy from respiration. The same nitrate, washed off a field into a river or lake, sets off a chain that ends with the water running out of oxygen.
can: Describe the root hair cell's extension and what it gives.
State the four points about active transport, and how osmosis differs.
Put the stages of eutrophication in order and name what uses the oxygen.

md: A root hair is one cell stretched into a thread between the soil grains. It drags mineral ions in against the flow, at a cost in energy, and the same ions washed into a river start a different story.

md: A **root hair cell** is a specialised cell with an **extended shape** — a single long, narrow projection that pushes out between the soil particles. Our cell body is about **60 micrometres** long and **20 micrometres** wide, but the hair itself reaches out around **700 micrometres**.

prompt: Why is a root hair cell drawn out into a long thread?
options: It gives the cell a much larger surface area
It lets the cell move through the soil
answer: It gives the cell a much larger surface area
explain: A long, narrow extension reaches between the soil grains and puts far more cell membrane in contact with the soil water.

md:
That extension gives an **increased surface area**, so **more mineral ions and more water can be absorbed at the same time**. Two different substances cross, in two completely different ways:

• **Mineral ions** (nitrate, for example) enter by **active transport**.
• **Water** enters by **osmosis**.

prompt: What does the root hair cell's extension give it?
options: a large surface area for absorption
answer: a large surface area for absorption
explain: A large surface area, so more water and more mineral ions can be absorbed at once. That is the phrase the mark scheme lists.

md: By the time a root has been growing for a while, the concentration of nitrate **inside** the cell is **higher** than in the soil water outside. Diffusion would therefore move nitrate **out**, which is no use to the plant. So the cell does the opposite: it moves the ions **against the concentration gradient**, from the **low** concentration outside to the **high** concentration inside. Going uphill needs **energy**, and that energy comes from **respiration**.

prompt: Nitrate is more concentrated inside the cell than in the soil water. Which way would diffusion move it?
options: it would not move at all
explain: Out, down the gradient — which is no use to the plant, so active transport carries it in instead.

title: Four things to say about active transport, every time
md:
**1** It moves **mineral ions** (not water).
**2** **Against** the concentration gradient — from **low to high** concentration.
**3** It **requires energy**.
**4** The energy comes from **respiration**.

And the fifth thing, which is what separates the marks: **water enters by osmosis, and osmosis needs no energy at all.**

options: from a low concentration to a high concentration, using energy from respiration
from a high concentration to a low concentration, using energy from respiration
from a high concentration to a low concentration, using no energy
answer: from a low concentration to a high concentration, using energy from respiration
explain: Low to high — against the gradient. Moving from high to low is diffusion, and it is free. Summer 2025 examiners reported many errors on exactly this direction.

md: This graph is the proof. With **no oxygen** the roots take up only **0.4 units** of nitrate; with plenty of oxygen they take up **7**. Oxygen is not part of a nitrate ion and does not carry it anywhere — what oxygen does is allow **aerobic respiration**, which **releases the energy** that active transport needs. The graph then **levels off**, because once respiration is at its maximum the roots cannot take up any more nitrate however much oxygen is supplied.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Active Transport"
why: Active transport against the gradient, with root hair cells as the worked example. Watch it, then answer the question underneath.

prompt: The energy used in active transport is released by ______.
explain: Respiration — aerobic respiration in the root hair cell's mitochondria. That is why waterlogged roots, starved of oxygen, take up so little nitrate.

title: PhET: Membrane Transport

task: Put a few particles on the outside and many on the inside, open a passive channel and watch which way they move. Then use the active-transport pump to move particles the other way. Write one sentence saying which of the two needed energy, and one sentence saying which one describes a root hair cell absorbing nitrate.

md: **What the nitrate is for.** Plants absorb **nitrates** and use them to make **amino acids** and then **proteins** — for growth, for enzymes, for everything. A plant short of nitrate grows poorly and its older leaves go pale, because it cannot build the protein it needs.

title: Magnesium is not on this specification
md: Many GCSE textbooks and videos teach **two** minerals: nitrate for protein and **magnesium for chlorophyll**. CCEA's Double Award B1 names only **nitrates, absorbed to make proteins** — magnesium appears nowhere in outcome 1.7.11 and has not appeared in a B1 paper. Know it if you like, but do not spend revision time on it, and do not offer it where the question asks for **the mineral required to make proteins**: that answer is **nitrate**.

prompt: Which mineral does this specification name as the one absorbed to make proteins?
explain: Nitrate. Magnesium belongs to other specifications, not to this outcome.

md:
**1** Fertiliser, slurry or untreated sewage is washed off the land into the water, adding nitrates (and phosphates).
**2** The extra nitrate makes algae and water plants grow and reproduce rapidly — an algal bloom.
**3** The bloom at the surface shades the plants below, and the nitrate is used up.
**4** Shaded and short of nitrate, the plants and algae die.

**5** Aerobic decomposing bacteria feed on the dead material and multiply.
**6** Those bacteria respire aerobically, so they use up the dissolved oxygen in the water.
**7** With little dissolved oxygen left, fish and aquatic invertebrates cannot respire, and they die.

prompt: Why do the water plants below an algal bloom die?
options: they are shaded and the nitrate runs out
answer: they are shaded and the nitrate runs out
explain: Shading and nitrate depletion — stages three and four.

title: Why 'less oxygen' — and why that is the step that kills
md: It is easy to think the algae themselves use up the oxygen. They do not: while they are alive they **photosynthesise** and put oxygen **in**. The oxygen crisis comes **after they die**. The **aerobic decomposing bacteria** feeding on all that dead material **multiply enormously**, and every one of them **respires aerobically**, taking **dissolved oxygen out of the water**. Fish and aquatic invertebrates need that dissolved oxygen for their own respiration, and when it runs out they suffocate. So the chain is: **dead algae → more bacteria → more aerobic respiration → less dissolved oxygen → animals die**.

prompt: Fish in a eutrophic lake die because they can no longer do what?
explain: Respire. Without dissolved oxygen there is no aerobic respiration.

title: Summer 2024 B1 Higher Q8 and Summer 2025 B1 Higher Q8
md: In Summer 2024 candidates had to put the stages in order: the examiners called it **strongly discriminating**, the order was **widely confused**, and answers that said **'nutrients' instead of nitrate or phosphate earned nothing** for that point. In Summer 2025 the same sequence was set as a diagram to complete: most candidates earned something, but **the last three stages proved the most difficult**. Learn the chain as causes, not as a list: each stage should start *because...*

prompt: What actually uses up the oxygen in a eutrophic lake?
options: aerobic bacteria respiring as they decompose the dead algae
the living algae, which use oxygen as they grow
the fish, because there are more of them
answer: aerobic bacteria respiring as they decompose the dead algae
explain: The decomposers. Living algae photosynthesise and add oxygen; it is the bacteria feeding on them after they die that strip it out.

prompt: Fertiliser run-off adds the ion ______ to a river, which makes algae grow rapidly.
explain: Nitrate (phosphate is also accepted). Summer 2024 examiners reported that the word 'nutrients' scored nothing here — the mark is for naming the ion.

md:
Describe the **root hair cell** and its **extension**.
State the four points about **active transport**: ions, against the gradient, energy, respiration.
Say that **water** enters by **osmosis**, needing no energy.
Name **nitrates** as the mineral used to make **proteins**.
Put the stages of **eutrophication** in order.

The root hair cell and its adaptation at Foundation; active transport and the whole of eutrophication at Higher, both of which have supplied a six-mark QWC recently. The schemes want the phrases: **against the concentration gradient**, **energy from respiration**, and the ion named. Stuck: name the ion and say which way it is moving.
